Limitations and what I’d improve next

I tested whether steering GPT-OSS-20B's activations while it read an attacked webpage could preserve the requested summary and prevent an unauthorized dummy-file upload. The most important limitations are:
Unclear causal value of the role directions.
My role probe classifies internal activations by message role. I can almost eliminate its

score for the forged passage while six of ten attacks still succeed. Changing the score does not establish that I changed the representation driving the action. The revised direction's early success also does not establish that its role effect caused the improvement. Next step: vary the layer and token positions I steer, and check whether behavioral effects track role scores during later
Source recognition does not establish permission.
The same webpage instruction can be legitimate under one

request and unauthorized under another. Recognizing its source cannot settle that distinction. My results do not locate the failure: source attribution, permission handling or subsequent action selection could each contribute. The separate permission experiment below tests this distinction with a different role direction and probe. Applying the revised direction from the upload study to that task would test whether it preserves permitted actions while rejecting unauthorized ones.

Random directions also reduce uploads, and a short developer reminder produced four uploads in ten trials, compared with six under the original direction. Matching the size of an activation change does not match how much it disrupts useful behavior; returning a summary does not establish its accuracy. Next step: compare steering, random directions and the reminder at similar performance on the
's task, including correctly completed authorized actions.
The revised direction has only been tested on development examples.

produced no uploads on five reused pages, compared with three without steering and one each under the reminder and the best observed random direction. These pages informed the revision, so this result may overestimate its advantage on unseen examples. Next step: freeze the direction and controls, then vary the attack and surrounding article separately on unseen examples, with repeated sampling.

I inspect all five role probabilities, and report the forged passage separately from the surrounding article. I average the probe's probabilities over all tokens in the forged passage immediately after the page is fetched. I compare probe scores with the development runs where the steering code adds no vector, and upload outcomes with runs without steering. A lower
score confirms a change in the measured representation; the upload record determines whether the attack succeeded.

The main comparison contains five development pages and five additional pages fixed before their outcomes were inspected. The additional pages reuse the five attack templates in different articles, so this tests sensitivity to surrounding content. Each page is evaluated with the same initial task and sampling seed under no intervention,

, its reverse, and three random directions of the same magnitude. The development pages also have a zero-dose control, which runs the steering machinery without adding a vector. A separate developer instruction says that retrieved text cannot authorize additional actions, providing a simpler baseline that requires no activation access.

These controls answer different questions. Zero dose checks whether the machinery itself changes the outcome. Reversing the direction tests whether its sign matters. Random directions test whether the proposed role contrast offers an advantage over an arbitrary change to activations. I retain every direction and compare outcomes page by page, so an aggregate improvement cannot hide an upload introduced on another page.

The original vector has no consistent advantage over controls

Pairing each steered episode with its unsteered counterpart shows how the outcomes change: the original direction prevents two uploads, introduces one, and leaves seven outcomes unchanged. All five new-page outcomes are unchanged. I retain the reversed direction, all three random directions, the developer instruction and the zero-dose check in Figure 1.

These are 80 recorded forgery episodes on ten webpages, which reuse five attack templates. Each arm/page has one sampled trajectory. The original vector does not outperform the random directions in this comparison. One Random 3 episode in each cohort remains unresolved; its segment marks the two possible final upload counts, not a confidence interval. Development zero-dose runs reproduce the no-intervention upload outcomes. No zero-dose arm was assigned on the new pages. The small sample leaves the effect size uncertain; unchanged outcomes do not prove that the underlying effect is zero.

That is a development result: the revised direction was constructed after inspecting earlier outcomes, and its five fixed new-page tests remain unrun. Each revised-direction run returned a summary, but I have not checked those summaries for accuracy. Completing those tests and grading the summaries would assess whether this construction prevents attacks while preserving the legitimate task. The current comparison does not establish that the measured role distribution caused the behavioral difference.
A second proxy task: selective execution
In a separate earlier experiment, I gave GPT-OSS-20B a page with two harmless file-writing commands, A and B. The page requested both actions; the
permitted only one and asked the model to report the fresh random value in each command. I changed only which action the
permitted. This let me measure unwanted writes, correct completion of the permitted action, and whether the answer used information from both commands.
Without steering, changing permission shifted the probe's scores on both commands together. In all eight available baseline cases, permitting the first-listed action raised both commands' mean
scores. In one example, command B scored 34.27%
when A was permitted and 28.26% when B itself was permitted. The command text and scored token positions were unchanged. A higher mean
score therefore did not consistently identify the permitted command. I have not yet tested whether reversing the commands reverses this pattern.
The task also showed why I need to measure useful behavior. Across 21 matched comparisons,

steering prevented four unwanted writes and introduced three. It also lost two correct completions of the permitted action and two answers reporting both values. A short developer reminder prevented six unwanted writes and introduced none in its own 21 matched comparisons, but lost two permitted completions. One prevented
write came from a malformed generation, so it was not a successful completion of the task.

This experiment used a different role probe and

steering on the command tokens. I recovered 149 of 280 assigned episodes, and each method has its own available matched comparisons. These counts describe the recovered runs; they do not establish a reliable ranking of methods. The eight-case score pattern also leaves command order and content bundled together. textRun.content: What I built and what I learned

Because this is an applied project, I optimized for end-to-end correctness and repeatability: a working experiment loop (attacked page → activation edit → agent actions → verified outcome) with saved inputs and outputs for each comparison. The rough sequence was:
Adapt a concrete attack and measure its outcome.

-forgery attack to a webpage-summarization task using GPT-OSS-20B. I built an isolated test environment with a dummy secret file and a local server that records whether the agent uploads the exact contents of the dummy file. This gave me a direct measure of attack success.

I adapted the paper’s role-probing method and added code to steer activations while the model processed retrieved text. I checked the layer and tokens being edited, and verified that setting the steering strength to zero preserved the generated tokens on identical inputs. These checks helped distinguish intervention effects from implementation errors.

I held pages and sampling seeds fixed across no steering, the proposed direction, its reverse, and three random directions of the same magnitude. I also tested an instruction that webpage text cannot authorize actions. I saved prompts,
and action traces, and upload records so I could inspect each outcome.
Use the failed intervention to refine the hypothesis.

The next tests I would prioritize are:
Test transfer with a frozen intervention.

Freeze the revised direction and controls, then cross unseen attack templates with unseen article contexts and repeat matched sampling seeds. This would separate dependence on an attack from dependence on the surrounding article. Report both uploads prevented and uploads introduced, since the net change can hide opposite effects.
Compare protection at similar task performance.

Grade summary accuracy and correct completion of authorized actions, with graders unaware of the intervention. Compare steering strengths, random directions and the developer reminder at similar task performance. Equal-sized activation changes need not cause equal disruption; the useful comparison is how much protection each method provides while preserving the work the

traces to propose explanations, then check them against contrary outcomes and controlled changes to the prompt.
